title: Correlation: Linearity, Outliers and Shared Variance
summary: Drag one observation and watch Pearson's r swing; change the units and watch it refuse to move. Then estimate r by eye for three plots and find out which way your error runs.
learningObjectives: State what Pearson's r does and does not measure.
Interpret r squared as the share of variance accounted for by the straight-line relationship, and say what the remainder is.
Explain why a near-zero correlation is not evidence of no relationship.
Describe how a single observation can dominate r in a small sample.
Distinguish a correlation from a regression slope and explain why one carries units.
interactionTypes: changing the units of the outcome
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every dataset is generated in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: Native ranges, selects, radio groups and buttons, each with an explicit label and grouped in a fieldset with a legend; the pull slider announces how far the ringed observation has been dragged and each estimate slider announces the correlation it currently reads. The scatterplot is hidden from assistive technology and paired inside its figure with a visible five-row table of n, r, r squared with its percentage, the slope in units of y per unit of x, and both standard deviations; a disclosure holds a three-column leave-one-out comparison. The moveable observation is marked with a ring - a shape rather than a colour - and each of the three challenge plots carries a written alternative beneath it describing how many points it holds and which way the cloud runs, so the eyeball test is answerable without seeing the picture. The pinned primary result measures 563px tall at 1366x768. Every dataset change, drag and unit change announces a full sentence through the polite live region, focus moves to the laboratory and challenge headings as they open, forced-colours rules are provided, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths with no horizontal page scroll.
readmeTopic: r measures straightness, not relatedness: curves, single points and a change of units
simulationNotes: All six datasets are generated by a seeded generator on a 0 to 100 frame, and x and y are deliberately unnamed so that no story does the explaining. The linear sets pair a standard normal x with a y correlated to a stated degree; the curve is a quadratic in x with a small amount of noise, giving a near-perfect relationship and a Pearson r of -0.01. The two odd-point sets use seeds chosen so that the generated cloud has a correlation near zero both with and without the ringed observation - 0.02 across all twelve and 0.08 across the other eleven - which is what makes the pull slider's effect entirely attributable to the one point it moves. Dragging that point to the corner takes r to 0.75 in the twelve-point set and to 0.04 in the hundred-and-twenty-point set. The units menu multiplies every y value by a constant, so the slope moves by exactly that factor - 0.87 becomes 8.69 or 0.17 - and r stays at 0.85, because the slope is r times the ratio of the standard deviations and therefore carries units. The challenge plots have correlations of 0.29, 0.86 and -0.63, and the feedback names the systematic underestimation of strong correlations rather than simply scoring the answers. Nothing here is real data, and no correlation on the page could establish causation.
